dossier.public_summary: The dip alternates odd/even and shows a second eclipse at a different phase, not expected for a planet. Many individual transits are too deep or missing entirely, and their depths change drastically between sectors, which is typical for a diluted eclipsing binary rather than a planet. A clear planetary signal is not the best explanation.

reasons.why: Odd 281.2 ppm vs even 543.1 ppm differ at 5.646 sigma with 48% difference, and sector_oe_max_sigma 14.04, best evidence for a binary at twice the period (25 d) rather than a planet at 12.5 d.
Secondary dip at phase 0.3568 with depth 92.11 ppm and depth_over_dip 0.23 is above the 5 threshold, not typical for a ~1.7 Rearth planet and indicates a stellar companion.

Depth changes 433.2% between sectors with chi2 473.8 dof 5; sector_depths_by_source verdict changes_within_a_source (p_constant_all 2.345e-101, SPOC p 1.24e-08, TESS-SPOC p 5.54e-95) shows real variation, not calibration, inconsistent with a stable planet.

10 of 11 individual transits inconsistent (top 3 carry 0.986 of signal): e.g. 1309 ppm sigma 13.9 vs -36 ppm sigma -7.1, confirming sector-to-sector depth change is transit-to-transit and not a planet.
Large phase-curve signal (33.78 ppm, ratio_to_depth 0.08414, chi2 18.39 dof 9) with brightening at secondary supports a close binary with ellipsoidal/thermal modulation, not a quiet planetary host.
